g1.label: 1. Drais’s machine was moved by the rider pushing against the ground with his feet.
g1.why: Paragraph B: the rider “sat on and pushed along the ground with his feet. There were no pedals.”

g2.label: 2. Drais’s first recorded ride took him several hours.
g2.why: Paragraph B: there and back “in a little over an hour” — not several hours.

g3.label: 3. Running machines cost more to buy than a horse.
g3.why: Paragraph B says the machines were “expensive” but never compares them with a horse.

g4.label: 4. On a high-wheeler, a bigger front wheel meant a greater distance for each turn of the pedals.
g4.why: Paragraph C: “the only way to travel further with every turn was to make the wheel bigger.”

g5.label: 5. In the 1870s, high-wheelers were popular with most women.
g5.why: Paragraph C: “most people, including most women, regarded the machine as far too dangerous to ride.”

g6.label: 6. Starley sold the Rover only in England.
g6.why: Paragraph D says Starley began selling the Rover in Coventry, but says nothing about where else it was sold.

g7.label: 7. A reason why riders of one design were often hurt
g7.why: Paragraph C: a stone or sudden stop “could throw him forward over the handlebars.”

g8.label: 8. A reference to an invention that was not taken up when it first appeared
g8.why: Paragraph E: Thomson’s 1845 tyre “was never developed for everyday use and was largely forgotten.”

g9.label: 9. An explanation of how ordinary-sized wheels could cover the same ground as very large ones
g9.why: Paragraph D: the chain from a large toothed wheel to a smaller one let “a wheel of ordinary size” travel as far as “a giant one”.

g10.label: 10. A mention of complaints about an early machine from members of the public
g10.why: Paragraph B: riders on crowded pavements were “regarded as a danger to people on foot.”

g11.label: 11. The Rover was given the name ___ because its rider sat low
g11.why: Paragraph D: “The design became known as the “safety bicycle”” — two words, copied exactly.

g12.label: 12. air-filled tyres replaced ___ ones
g12.why: Paragraph E: “Solid rubber tyres passed every bump in the road straight to the rider.”

g13.label: 13. travel alone, without a ___ to supervise them
g13.why: Paragraph F: “without a horse, a carriage or a chaperone” — only a chaperone supervises a person.

g1.label: 14. Heading for paragraph A
g1.why: Paragraph A explains why the colony needs information “shared inside the hive”; vi only echoes the detail about flowers.

g2.label: 15. Heading for paragraph B
g2.why: Paragraph B: “the dance turned a direction and a distance into a pattern of movement.”

g3.label: 16. Heading for paragraph C
g3.why: Paragraph C covers both problems: the dance “takes place in near darkness” and bees “adjust the angle … as the day goes on.”

g4.label: 17. Heading for paragraph D
g4.why: Paragraph D: Wenner argued that recruits “found food by smell”; the Nobel Prize (iii) is only a detail.

g5.label: 18. Heading for paragraph E
g5.why: Paragraph E: experiments “in which the dance and the smell could be separated.”

g6.label: 19. Heading for paragraph F
g6.why: Paragraph F: the dance is “one important tool” used “with other cues, including scent.”

g11.label: 24. Von Frisch received his Nobel Prize after Wenner’s challenge had begun.
g11.why: Paragraph D: the 1973 prize came when “it had already been seriously challenged” — Wenner’s challenge began in 1967.

g12.label: 25. The robot bee recruited more bees than a real dancer.
g12.why: Paragraph E says real bees followed the robot’s direction, but never compares how many it recruited with a real dancer.

g13.label: 26. Experienced foragers always follow the most recent dance they meet.
g13.why: Paragraph F: experienced foragers “sometimes ignore dances entirely.”

g7.label: 20. In a waggle run, the bee shakes her body while moving in a ___.
g7.why: Paragraph B: “the bee moves forward in a straight line while shaking her body.”

g8.label: 21. Bees following a dance sense it through contact and through ___ and vibrations.
g8.why: Paragraph C: “through contact and through the air currents and vibrations that she produces.”

g9.label: 22. According to Wenner, recruits used the scent on the dancer’s body and ___ along the route.
g9.why: Paragraph D: “the scent of the flowers clinging to the dancer’s body together with odours along the route.”

g10.label: 23. In 2005, researchers followed recruits’ flights by attaching tiny ___ to them.
g10.why: Paragraph E: researchers “fitted recruit bees with tiny radar transponders.”

g1.label: 27. A method that showed knowledge had survived even when none of it came to mind
g1.why: Paragraph B: savings revealed traces of learning “even when he could not produce a single syllable.”

g2.label: 28. A reason to doubt whether an early result applies to people in general
g2.why: Paragraph C: “the original study had a single participant.”

g3.label: 29. Evidence that learners can misjudge how much they will retain
g3.why: Paragraph E: restudying students “felt more confident” but remembered less after a delay.

g4.label: 30. A suggestion that effective methods may be unpopular with the people who would benefit
g4.why: Paragraph F: spaced and retrieval practice “feel harder than rereading, so students may resist them.”

g5.label: 31. the ___ of practice sessions affected memory
g5.why: Paragraph D: “the way practice is arranged matters” — spreading sessions out, not adding more.

g6.label: 32. repetitions spread over several days led to better ___

g7.label: 33. Later research has ___ this finding many times
g7.why: Paragraph D: the spacing effect “has been confirmed many times since.”

g8.label: 34. Retrieval practice works in a less ___ way
g8.why: Paragraph E: retrieval practice “works in a less obvious way.”

g9.label: 35. those who had ___ themselves remembered more a week later
g9.why: Paragraph E: students who took “a test” in which they recalled the passages remembered more after a week.

g10.label: 36. despite feeling less ___ about it
g10.why: Paragraph E: the students who restudied “felt more confident”, so the tested students felt less confident.

g11.label: 37. Ebbinghaus used ___ so that meaning would not affect his results.
g11.why: Paragraph A: “he invented thousands of nonsense syllables.”

g12.label: 38. Ebbinghaus’s book on memory was published in ___.
g12.why: Paragraph A: his findings were “published in 1885.”

g13.label: 39. The participant in the 2015 study spent about ___ learning and relearning lists.
g13.why: Paragraph C: “One participant spent about seventy hours learning and relearning lists.”

g14.label: 40. Bjork calls techniques that are effortful but effective “___”.
g14.why: Paragraph F: Bjork “has described techniques of this kind as “desirable difficulties”.”
